learn.canDo: Explain why a B-tree lookup stays cheap as a table grows, and choose indexes by what the queries ask and what writes will pay.
learn.why: A missing index is the most common cause of a slow query, and too many indexes quietly slow every write. Interviewers expect both halves.
learn.keyIdea: Depth grows with the log; every index taxes writes.

learn.canDo: Read an EXPLAIN plan, spot the expensive node, and design a composite or covering index that removes it.
learn.why: An index that exists is not an index that is used. Reading the plan is how you find out why a query is slow and prove your fix.
learn.keyIdea: Equality columns first, then the sort column.

learn.canDo: Decide per column whether to join, copy, or cache, by comparing how often it is read with how often it changes.
learn.why: Join-heavy feeds are slow and copied columns drift. The choice is a trade of read speed for write cost, made one fact at a time.
learn.keyIdea: Copy what is read hot and changes cold.

learn.canDo: Use a transaction to make multi-step changes atomic, and explain how the write-ahead log makes commits durable.
learn.why: A crash between two statements is a real incident, and money or orders silently vanish. Atomicity and durability are the first things you check.
learn.keyIdea: Log first, pages later; commit means the log is on disk.

learn.canDo: Name the anomalies each isolation level permits, and choose between Serializable and explicit row locks.
learn.why: Double bookings and negative stock come from races that pass every unit test. Matching the tool to the anomaly is a staple of design interviews.
learn.keyIdea: Different rows, shared rule: that is write skew.

learn.canDo: Explain row versions and vacuum, and find why a table is bloated when one long transaction is the cause.
learn.why: Bloat and slow scans on update-heavy Postgres tables usually trace back to something holding a snapshot open, not to vacuum settings.
learn.keyIdea: Vacuum cannot remove what an old snapshot might see.

learn.canDo: Match a workload to relational, key-value, document, wide-column, or graph storage by its access pattern and guarantees.
learn.why: Choosing a database by fashion is expensive to undo. Starting from the access pattern is the habit interviewers look for.
learn.keyIdea: Match the store to the access pattern.

learn.canDo: Compare B-tree and LSM storage by write, read, and space amplification, and say what compaction costs.
learn.why: Write-heavy systems choose engines by how many bytes hit the disk per row. Knowing the three amplifications explains most storage engine choices.
learn.keyIdea: Append and merge: cheap writes, paid for by compaction.

learn.canDo: Decide when Postgres can carry a workload and when a measured load justifies one more system, adding them one at a time.
learn.why: Every new datastore is a permanent operating cost. 'Start boring and justify each addition' is both good engineering and a good interview answer.
learn.keyIdea: Each extra system needs a measured reason.

learn.canDo: Combine indexes, locking, short holds, and replica reports to run a ticket sale that never sells a seat twice.
learn.why: A sale puts every database fundamental under pressure at once. Choosing which tool fixes which failure is the skill.
learn.keyIdea: Hold locks for milliseconds, not through payment.

chapter.story: Pigeon's Postgres starts to sweat, and every shortcut taken earlier shows up in the query log.
outcomes: Choose indexes and read EXPLAIN plans
Decide when to join, copy, or cache a column
Use transactions and isolation levels to prevent races
Explain MVCC, vacuum, and bloat; compare B-trees and LSM trees; know when Postgres is enough
chapter.why: The database is where most systems finally hit their limits, and where mistakes are hardest to undo. This chapter turns indexes, transactions, and storage into numbers you can reason about.
chapter.payoff: In an interview you can design a schema, name the index, and say what isolation level a booking needs. At work you will read a slow-query log and know where to look.
